verdict.reasoning: Patient reports shortness of breath for about an hour while resting and watching TV: 'over the last hour, I've started to feel, like, a bit short of breath.' and doctor confirms 'you've noticed shortness of breath for just an hour, while sitting and watching TV?'

Patient describes a cough starting yesterday and denies expectoration: 'I started with a cough yesterday.' and in response to whether she has brought anything up: 'Uh, no, I haven't, no.' This supports a dry cough since yesterday with no sputum.

Palpitations: 'my heart, it's really going.' and doctor: 'So, you're feeling your heart more than normal?' Chest pain denied: 'And, the shortness of breath, does it cause any pain in your chest?'; patient: 'Um, no.' Chest soreness on deep inspiration: 'How about when you take a very deep breath in?' patient: 'Um, I mean, yeah. My chest feels sore...'
Patient notes C-section scar is tender: 'my chest feels sore, but so does my C-section scar. You know, it's, it's all tender.'
Patient denies previous similar episodes: 'And, have you noticed anything like this before?' Patient: 'Um, no.'
Timing of C-section: Patient: 'I had a C-section a few weeks ago.' Doctor: 'And, how long ago was that? Just a few weeks?' Patient: 'Yeah, four weeks.'
Post-op Codeine use and last dose: Patient: 'they gave me some, uh, Codeine.' and 'I, I've been taking that fairly, fairly regularly. But, probably haven't taken it for a week.'

Ibuprofen allergy with unspecified reaction: Patient: 'I'm allergic to Ibuprofen, though.' When asked what happens, she responds: 'I don't know. Sorry.' This indicates allergy with unspecified reaction.
Family history: Patient states, 'my mum's had, uh, clots in her legs before.'

Postpartum and alone with newborn, partner at work: She had a C-section 4 weeks ago (postpartum) and 'are you with baby at the moment?' 'Yes, I am.' and later 'Is anyone else with you at home?' Patient: 'Uh, no. My partner's at work.'

Acute postpartum SOB with concern for PE: The scenario is acute postpartum SOB. Doctor expresses concern for clots in lungs: 'what I'm worried about at the moment is, given that you've had a C-section... Some people can suffer with clots... in your lungs.' and recommends hospital to get checked out. This supports query pulmonary embolism as the working concern.

Tachycardia attributed to SOB/pain/stress: After pulse count, doctor says, 'So, your heart is running slightly fast at the moment, which is probably because of the shortness of breath and some of the pain that you're under.' Patient also notes feeling stressed. This supports tachycardia likely secondary to SOB, pain, or anxiety/stress.
Post-operative status 4 weeks post C-section is documented: 'I had a C-section a few weeks ago.' 'Yeah, four weeks.'
Ibuprofen allergy is explicitly noted: Patient: 'I'm allergic to Ibuprofen, though.'

Immediate ED referral and self-transport with baby are supported, but calling 999 if deterioration is not mentioned. Doctor offers ambulance vs self-transport: 'I can call an ambulance. Or, you can take yourself to the hospital with baby.' Patient chooses self-transport. The instruction 'call 999 if there is deterioration' does not appear in the transcript.
Doctor instructs to hold Codeine: 'And, if you're taking any medications like Codeine, don't, don't take them for the time being.'

Doctor educates about postpartum clot risk and hospital process: 'given that you've had a C-section... Some people can suffer with clots... in your lungs.' 'It's quite a common thing to happen. And, it's not something to worry about. But, needs to be checked out in the hospital first.' and 'if that does become the case, they can give you something to reduce the clot... Fairly quick process.'

No instruction is given to update partner or to return for emergent care if symptoms worsen en route. Closest is general advice to go quickly: 'go fairly quickly and take some bits for baby at the same time.'

Radial pulse assessed as fast: Doctor guides patient to feel wrist pulse, times it, and patient reports 'I counted thirty' over a set interval. Doctor concludes, 'So, your heart is running slightly fast at the moment,' indicating tachycardia.
